subject: chem
title: Group 2
subtitle: Reactions, trends and uses of Group 2 elements and compounds.
concept: Group 2 elements (Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) lose 2 electrons to form M²⁺ ions; reactivity increases down the group as IE decreases.
Group 2 oxides and hydroxides are bases; they neutralise acids and are used industrially.
Solubility trends: sulfates become less soluble down the group; hydroxides become more soluble.

notes.heading: Reactions of Group 2 Metals
items: Reaction with oxygen: 2M + O₂ → 2MO (burns brightly; Mg burns intensely white).
Reaction with water: Mg reacts slowly with hot water/steam (MgO + H₂); Ca, Sr, Ba react with cold water → M(OH)₂ + H₂.
Reaction with dilute acid: M + H₂SO₄ → MSO₄ + H₂ (MgSO₄ soluble; CaSO₄ sparingly soluble — may slow reaction due to insoluble layer).
Ca reacts more vigorously than Mg — lower IE, metal is more easily oxidised.

notes.heading: Oxides and Hydroxides
items: All Group 2 oxides are basic: MO + H₂O → M(OH)₂ (CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, exothermic — quicklime/slaked lime).
MgO: refractory material (very high MP ~2852°C); used in furnace linings.
Ca(OH)₂: used to neutralise acidic soil, treat sewage, make glass.
CaCO₃ (limestone): quarried; heated to give CaO (lime) — used in steelmaking and pH control of soil.
Thermal decomposition: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Ease of decomposition decreases down the group (higher T needed for BaCO₃).

notes.heading: Solubility Trends
items: Group 2 sulfates: MgSO₄ (soluble) → CaSO₄ (sparingly) → SrSO₄ (insoluble) → BaSO₄ (insoluble). Solubility decreases down the group.
Group 2 hydroxides: Mg(OH)₂ (sparingly soluble) → Ca(OH)₂ (slightly) → Ba(OH)₂ (soluble). Solubility increases down the group.
BaSO₄: used in barium meal (X-ray contrast agent) — insoluble so not absorbed; opaque to X-rays.
Test for SO₄²⁻ ions: add BaCl₂(aq) acidified with HCl → white precipitate of BaSO₄ (HCl prevents carbonate/sulfite interference).

definitions.body: A reaction in which a compound breaks down when heated into simpler substances.
Sulfates become less soluble down Group 2; hydroxides become more soluble down Group 2.

workedExamples.q: Explain the trend in reactivity of Group 2 metals with water down the group.

steps.text: Ca reacts vigorously with cold water; Mg only reacts with hot water/steam. Reactivity increases Ca > Mg.
Down the group, atomic radius increases and shielding increases → outer electrons further from nucleus → lower first and second IE.
Easier to lose the 2 outer electrons → more reactive metal → reacts more readily with water.

mistakes: Saying Group 2 hydroxide solubility decreases down the group — it increases (Ba(OH)₂ is most soluble).
Using dilute HNO₃ instead of HCl when testing for sulfate — HNO₃ is an oxidising acid that can interfere.
tips: Barium meal uses BaSO₄ — INSOLUBLE, not absorbed → safe to ingest; BaCl₂ would be toxic.
Thermal stability of carbonates: increases down group (more difficult to decompose BaCO₃ than MgCO₃).
Flame colours: Mg (no characteristic); Ca (brick red); Sr (crimson); Ba (pale green).

flashcards.q: What is the trend in solubility of Group 2 hydroxides down the group?
flashcards.a: Solubility increases — Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ is soluble.

flashcards.q: Why is BaSO₄ used in barium meals (X-ray imaging)?
flashcards.a: BaSO₄ is insoluble and not absorbed through the gut (non-toxic); it is opaque to X-rays, showing up the digestive tract.

flashcards.q: Write the equation for thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
Why does reactivity of Group 2 metals increase down the group?
flashcards.a: Atomic radius increases; outer electrons are more shielded and further from nucleus → lower IE → easier to lose 2e⁻.

flashcards.q: What is the test for sulfate ions?
flashcards.a: Add BaCl₂(aq) acidified with HCl → white precipitate of BaSO₄ (insoluble).

flashcards.q: What is the trend in Group 2 sulfate solubility?
flashcards.a: Decreases down the group: MgSO₄ soluble; BaSO₄ insoluble.

questions.q: Which Group 2 hydroxide is most soluble?
questions.exp: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group — Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble.

questions.q: What is formed when CaO reacts with water?
questions.exp: CaO (quicklime) + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime); exothermic reaction.

questions.q: The trend in thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates down the group is:
questions.exp: Thermal stability increases down the group — BaCO₃ requires higher temperatures to decompose than MgCO₃.

questions.q: How is sulfate ion confirmed in solution?
opts: Add BaCl₂(aq) acidified with HCl → white precipitate
questions.exp: BaCl₂ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ (white precipitate); acidified with HCl to remove interfering CO₃²⁻ and SO₃²⁻.

questions.q: Why does barium sulfate (not barium chloride) used in X-ray imaging?
opts: BaSO₄ is more opaque to X-rays
BaSO₄ is insoluble and non-toxic; BaCl₂ is soluble and toxic
BaSO₄ dissolves slowly in the stomach
questions.exp: BaSO₄ is insoluble — not absorbed into the bloodstream, so it's non-toxic. BaCl₂ is soluble and would be toxic.
